column4: The source section's dictionary form البعير المعبد means a subdued camel; this ayah says God subdued the sacrificial animals so people would magnify Him for the guidance He gave them. It brings the animal's submission, worship, and هدى together.

The source section's root س م و explains اسم as a name that raises the named one's remembrance; here God's name is recited over the standing sacrificial camels, which are then slaughtered and shared as food.
The source section links أنعمت to the herd word الأنعام through root ن ع م; this ayah names livestock as God's provision and commands that His name be remembered over them.

The section's source root س م و concerns the name raised over the offered animal, and its root ن ع م names the herd; this ayah joins God's name, livestock He provided, appointed days, eating, and feeding the poor.
The source section's dictionary word الهدي is a sacrificial animal led to its appointed place; this ayah says its destination is the Ancient House, البيت العتيق.
The source section quotes this very rule: complete Hajj and Umrah, and do not release the pilgrim state until الهدي reaches its محل, its appointed place.
The source section's dictionary form الهدي is an offering; this ayah specifies an offering that reaches the Kaaba, الهديا بالغ الكعبة, in the rule for a hunting violation during pilgrimage.
The section's الهدي is meant to reach its محل; here the offerings are held back from reaching that place while the believers are barred from the Sacred Mosque, a direct interruption of both arrivals.
The source section says the offering and a person seeking protection are inviolable; this ayah forbids violating الهدي, the garlanded offerings, or those heading to the Sacred House.
The section brings the sacrificial animal to a House and links it to the Hajj season; this ayah makes the Sacred Kaaba, sacred month, offerings, and garlands a standing for people.
The section treats the Hady as inviolable; this ayah says honoring God's sha'a'ir is from the piety of hearts, giving the animal's protected status a devotional meaning.

After 22:34 names God over livestock, this ayah describes the response when God is mentioned: hearts tremble, and the people pray, endure, and give. Its contribution is the worshipper's stance beside the offering rite.
This ayah assigns every community a rite so its people mention God's name over livestock He provided, then tells them to submit to the one God; it directly joins herd, offering, and service.
The section's animal is taken to the House as قربى and serves worship; here Abraham is told to purify God's House for those who circle it, stand, bow, and prostrate.
The section's guidance image has a road ending at a House; this ayah calls people to Hajj and pictures them arriving on foot and on lean camels from distant passes.
Following the Hajj call and offerings in 22:27-28, this ayah completes the approach with vows and circumambulation of the Ancient House; it supplies the arriving pilgrim's destination and rite.
The section makes the Hady sacred and protected; this ayah says to honor God's sanctities and distinguishes lawful livestock from what has been recited as forbidden.
The section says the offering is قربى إلى الله; this ayah uses قربانا for the offering of Adam's two sons and distinguishes what God accepts from what He does not.

The section's stated purpose is قربى to God through an offering; this ayah reports the rejected claim that worshipping other protectors will bring people nearer to God, exposing a rival route to nearness.
The section's قربى is directed to God; this ayah calls the false gods taken as قربانا useless when their worshippers need help, reversing the promised nearness.
On the sacrificial reading of وَانْحَرْ, this command pairs prayer with an offering directed to your Lord, matching the section's animal brought near through worship.
The source section's root ه د ي includes showing a road and bringing someone to a house; as Moses travels toward Midian, he says, عسى ربي أن يهديني سواء السبيل, asking for guidance along the way.

Moses reaches the water of Midian, where shepherds water their flocks and two women hold theirs back; this supplies the herd, herdsmen, and roadside meeting that the section's gift, bride, and refuge images can meet.
Moses waters the women's flock, then turns to shade and asks his Lord for whatever good He sends; the verse joins care for a herd to a request for provision and hospitality.
One of the women comes to Moses and brings him toward her father's household, offering a reward for watering the flock; this meets the section's led-to-a-home and gift-for-kindness images.
After the invitation in 28:25, the woman describes Moses as strong and trustworthy; this is the household's stated reason for receiving him and considering him for the marriage that follows.

The section says the bride is led to her husband's home after nikah; here the father proposes marriage to one daughter on an agreed term of service, explicitly joining marriage and a binding arrangement.
Moses accepts the marriage term and says God is witness to their agreement; this completes 28:27 and meets the section's covenant as the bond that secures a person received into a household.
The source section's root ه د ي appears here in هداني ربي إلى صراط مستقيم; the ayah names Abraham's upright way as the destination of God's guidance.
Immediately after the guided path in 6:161, Abraham says his prayer and sacrifice, life and death are for God; this directly joins the section's worship with its offering.
The section glosses worship as obedience; Abraham is described here as قانتا لله, devotedly obedient to God, in the same Abrahamic setting as pilgrimage and offering.
The source section links root ن ع م in أنعمت to livestock; this ayah uses the same favor-family for Abraham, then says God chose and guided him to a straight path.
The source section identifies النعم as camels and livestock; this ayah says God created cattle for warmth, benefits, and food, making the herd from which the Hady is drawn visible as provision.

The adjoining ayah describes the herd as beautiful when brought home in the evening and driven out in the morning; it gives an everyday return-and-departure scene behind the animal led away to the House.
This ayah shows livestock carrying people's burdens to distant land; the section reverses that direction, with the camel itself led on a journey to its sacred destination.
The source section's herd word is الأنعام; this ayah divides livestock into burden-bearing and other kinds, then calls it God's provision to eat, showing the same animals as transport and food.

The source section uses root م ل ك for marriage; here فَهُمْ لَهَا مَالِكُونَ uses its ownership sense for livestock, making explicit that the herd from which an offering is taken is also held by people.
The source section's dictionary form البعير المعبد means a tamed camel; this ayah says God ذللناها, subdued livestock for people to ride and eat, a close parallel in sense.
The section describes a subdued camel set on a journey; this riding prayer says to remember the Lord's favor and glorify the One who subjected the mount.
The riding prayer begun in 43:13 ends here with إنا إلى ربنا لمنقلبون, naming the journey's return to the Lord; it echoes the section's claim that a road has a destination.
The section's dictionary says the Hady may be a camel; this ayah specifically turns attention to camels and how they were created, keeping the actual animal in view beyond its ritual role.
The section protects the Hady and those headed to the House; Salih's she-camel is declared a sign and must be left unharmed, another camel whose sacred status forbids interference.
Salih calls his she-camel a sign and commands his people to leave her grazing in God's land without harm; this parallels the section's protected offering animal.
The people hamstring Salih's protected she-camel, the direct reversal of the section's inviolable Hady; the following warning makes the consequence of violating that boundary explicit.

The section's Hady is a divinely named offering; this ayah rejects self-invented livestock taboos such as bahira and saiba, marking a boundary between prescribed offering and invented animal sanctity.
The source section draws النعم from the same root family as أنعمت; this ayah calls heedless people like cattle, even more astray, reversing the blessed and guided people of the image.

The source section links the livestock word الأنعام to أنعمت; here people who do not listen or reason are compared to cattle and called more astray in the way, a pointed reversal of the requested guidance.
The source section's herd animal is provision brought in worship; this ayah contrasts believers' promised Garden with disbelievers who eat like cattle and have the Fire as their abode.
The section says God's name is spoken over the sacrificial animal; this ayah permits eating what has had God's name mentioned over it.
Where 6:118 permits food over which God's name was mentioned, this ayah forbids eating what lacks that mention; it marks the boundary around the section's named offering.
This ayah permits game caught by trained hunting animals and commands ذكر اسم الله عليه; it parallels the section's tamed animal and the name that accompanies food.
The section places God's name over its offering; this ayah forbids what was dedicated to other than God, stating the opposite boundary for an animal's consecration.
The source section's root س م و describes the raised remembrance carried by a name; this ayah joins houses raised by God's leave with His name being remembered in them.
The source section says the name raises the named one's remembrance; this command explicitly says سَبِّحِ اسْمَ رَبِّكَ الْأَعْلَى, joining the name to glorification and exaltation.
The section's path reaches a House; this ayah identifies the first House at Bakkah as blessed and guidance for all worlds.
The section describes the House as a destination and the refugee as protected; this ayah says whoever enters the House is safe and makes pilgrimage to it a duty.
The House is made مَثَابَةً لِّلنَّاسِ وَأَمْنًا, a return and safety for people; the same ayah records God's covenant with Abraham and Ishmael to purify it.
Abraham asks God to make the city secure and provide its people with fruits; it joins the section's safe destination with the herd and gift as provision.
After the House is declared a place of return and safety in 2:125, Abraham and Ishmael raise its foundations and ask God to accept their service; this adds the act of preparing the destination.

Abraham settles his family by the Sacred House so they can establish prayer, asks that people's hearts incline toward them, and asks for provision; this joins home, worship, and being drawn toward the House.
This command names the Lord of this House as the one to worship, directly meeting the section's link between the House, service, and devotion.
The same passage says the Lord fed the people against hunger and made them safe from fear; it gives food and sanctuary safety as gifts of the House's Lord.
This ayah says God made the sanctuary secure while people around it were being seized; it clarifies the House's protective boundary that the section extends to a person seeking refuge.
After the offerings are held back in 48:25, this ayah promises entry into the Sacred Mosque safely and without fear, completing the interrupted road to the House.
The section's destination offers protection and provision; this ayah pictures a secure, provisioned town losing both after ingratitude, a reversal of shelter as a gift.
This ayah joins the section's two images in one sentence: God invites people to دار السلام and guides whom He wills to a straight path.
The source section asks for guidance to a destination; following the account of those killed in God's cause, this ayah says God will guide them and set their condition right.
The next ayah completes 47:5 by saying God will admit them to the Paradise He has made known to them, giving guidance a home at its end.
The source section asks اهدنا الصراط المستقيم; this ayah says God would guide people to a straight path, closely matching the plea's wording and action.
Following the straight-path promise in 4:68, this ayah identifies the companions as those God has favored, echoing the source phrase أنعمت عليهم in its human, not livestock, sense.
The source section's dictionary calls the Hajj season a marker where people gather; this ayah says the new moons are appointed times for people and Hajj, a calendar marker for that gathering.
The source section makes the Hajj season a marked time of gathering; this ayah calls Hajj's months known, giving the season a defined calendar place.
This Hajj passage names المشعر الحرام, the sacred landmark, and tells pilgrims to remember God there after leaving Arafat; it closely matches the section's season-as-marker and gathering.
This ayah calls Safa and Marwa signs of God and places them in Hajj and Umrah, making pilgrimage's marked route visible.
The section's season is a marker where people gather; this ayah has a public announcement to people on the day of the greater Hajj.
The section says the bride is led to her husband's household after marriage; this ayah orders that women's dowries be given as a gift, نِحْلَةً, in that marriage bond.
The source section's dictionary branch for root ر ب ب names a covenant, and its bride is joined through marriage; this ayah calls marriage a مِيثَاقًا غَلِيظًا, a solemn covenant.
The section's dictionary says a bride is gathered to her husband and joined to him; this ayah says a spouse is made so he may find rest with her, لِيَسْكُنَ إِلَيْهَا.
The section's gift is offered to one with mawadda; this ayah says God placed affection and mercy between spouses, giving the bride's household a relationship of affection.
Believing women arrive as emigrants and must not be returned to disbelievers; the ayah then permits marriage to them with their dowries, joining refuge, a new household, and the bride's transfer.
The source section's dictionary form الهدية is a gift sent to someone; here the Queen says she will send a هدِيَّة to Solomon and wait for the envoys' return.
Solomon rejects the Queen's هديتكم and says they rejoice in their gift; unlike the section's gift to a beloved recipient, this gift to a rival does not reach its intended home.
The queen's warning that kings corrupt cities and humble their honored people frames why she sends the gift in 27:35; this verse contributes the political danger behind that failed offering.
After rejecting the gift in 27:36, Solomon orders the envoys returned; this confirms that the gift is sent back and the road to its recipient is closed.
This ayah directly stages the section's protected stranger: if a polytheist asks for refuge, protect him, let him hear God's word, then deliver him to his safe place, مَأْمَنَهُ.
Following the asylum rule in 9:6, this ayah speaks of treaties at the Sacred Mosque and commands fairness while the other party keeps its terms, linking protection to a kept covenant.
The source section's dictionary branch for ر ب ب explains protection through covenant; this ayah orders treaties with those who have kept faith to be honored until their agreed term.
This ayah protects people who join a community with a covenant or come offering peace; it says not to fight them if they withdraw, matching the section's shelter and safe-conduct image.
Believers who gave emigrants shelter and support are named as allies; this is a community receiving people who have left home, parallel to the section's protected arrival.
The ayah promises that whoever emigrates for God will find much refuge and abundance on earth, then speaks of death arriving on the road; it makes migration's shelter and destination explicit.
The youths take refuge in the cave and ask their Lord for mercy and a rightly ordered outcome; this is another explicit request for shelter and guidance from within it.
After the youths withdraw from their people, this ayah tells them to take refuge in the cave and promises mercy and a prepared outcome, completing the shelter scene of 18:10.
This ayah describes emigrants driven from their homes and property who seek God's bounty and pleasure; it supplies the displaced travel behind the section's seeker of protection.
The next ayah describes the people settled in the abode and faith who love those migrating to them and prefer them; it shows the welcoming household that completes 59:8.
The source section's dictionary branch for ر ب ب treats a bond as an عهد and ميثاق; this ayah commands people to fulfill God's covenant and not break oaths after confirming them.
The section's refugee seeks a safe place in order to be protected; this ayah says hypocrites would rush to any refuge, cave, or hiding place to evade obligation, a morally opposite use of shelter.
Pharaoh's wife asks her Lord to build her a house near Him in Paradise and save her from Pharaoh and wrongdoing people; it joins a woman's household, refuge, and final safe home.
The source section's root ه د ي includes showing a road and bringing someone to a house; this ayah says God laid roads in the earth so people may be guided along them.
The source section develops ma'lam as a marker where people gather and connects it to hidaya; this ayah pairs landmarks, علامات, with being guided by the stars.
This ayah says God made the stars so people may find their way through the darkness of land and sea, a concrete navigation scene for the section's dictionary sense of showing someone a road.
The source section asks for guidance to a straight path that reaches a home; this ayah says God guides those seeking His pleasure to paths of peace and then to a straight path.
This ayah says the Lord guides believers by their faith and has rivers flow beneath them in gardens, a direct progression from guidance to a destination of repose.
After 6:118 permits food over which God's name was mentioned, this ayah asks why people would not eat it and states the exception for compulsion; it continues the named-food rule in its own context.
This ayah says the Sacred Mosque is for resident and visitor alike and warns against hindering access; it gives a boundary around the House to which the section's offering and pilgrim are headed.

This ayah bars polytheists from approaching the Sacred Mosque after that year, setting a limit on access to the sanctuary beside 9:6's temporary protection and safe escort for a polytheist seeking refuge.
This ayah describes people assigning portions of crops and livestock to God and partners, then misdirecting those portions; it reverses the section's animal sincerely offered as قربى to God.

This ayah reports a demand for a قربان consumed by fire as proof from a messenger, together with a claimed covenant; unlike the section's devotional Hady, the offering is made a test for rejecting messengers.
This ayah says Abraham's son was ransomed with a great sacrifice, a distinct sacrificial scene that shows an animal offering taking another's place in Abraham's story.
The disciples ask Jesus whether his Lord can send down a table from heaven; this is a specific offered-table scene parallel to the section's dictionary sense of a gift carried on a platter.
The disciples say they want to eat from the table and have their hearts reassured; this states the recipients' need within the table-gift scene begun in 5:112.
Jesus asks God to send a table from heaven as a feast and sign and asks Him to provide for them; it develops the section's secondary tray-and-gift image as a divine provision.
God says He will send the table, then warns of severe punishment for disbelief afterward; this completes the gift scene with the boundary attached to refusing its sign.
After the Arafat landmark in 2:198, this ayah tells pilgrims to depart from where the people depart and seek forgiveness, adding the movement of the gathered Hajj crowd.
This ayah says that after completing the rites pilgrims should remember God; it continues the Hajj season's gathering and links its marked days to the named remembrance developed in the section.
In the same Hajj passage, this ayah gives the petition for good in this life and the Hereafter and protection from the Fire, a prayer for provision and a safe final destination.
The Hajj passage returns to remembrance of God on numbered days; this gives the season's marker a fixed ritual calendar and continues the gathering beyond Arafat.
This ayah sets the year at twelve months with four sacred months, a calendar boundary for the section's marked Hajj season and inviolable offerings.
This ayah condemns moving the sacred months from their appointed places; it marks the boundary against shifting the season that the section treats as a sign for gathering.
The source section's dictionary branch for root ر ب ب describes a bond as covenant; this ayah commands people to fulfill their covenant and says they will be questioned about it.
The source section connects protection with عهد and ميثاق; this ayah identifies believers by their care for trusts and covenants, the reliability that makes a refuge promise meaningful.
Following the shelter and support described in 8:72, this ayah again joins emigrants with those who give them refuge and promises forgiveness and honorable provision to them.

This ayah depicts people who remain in an oppressive land being asked why they did not migrate; it contrasts with the section's seeker who is led out to a safe place, while the following verses exempt those unable to leave.
This ayah describes the God-fearing being led in groups until they arrive at the Garden and its gates open, a clear scene of a guided road reaching a home.
After arrival in 39:73, the Garden's people praise God for fulfilling His promise and giving them the land as inheritance; it supplies the welcomed residents' account of reaching their home.
This ayah places the righteous with their spouses and families in gardens they enter through the gates, joining the section's bride-and-house image to a final home.
The next ayah gives the angels' greeting of peace to those entering the Garden; it completes the household-arrival scene in 13:23 with a safe welcome.

The source section's root و س م includes marking or branding and uses the Hajj season as a landmark; this ayah uses its concrete branding sense on a person's snout, a harsh mark unlike a marker that gathers people.
This ayah identifies Salih's camel as God's and names her watering turn; it adds another protected camel scene beside the section's inviolable Hady.
The people hamstring the she-camel in 91:13 and their Lord destroys them for it, a direct violation of the protected animal's boundary.
